newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's North enters iron ore big league.
newsitem.headline: Australia's North enters iron ore big league.

text.p: Australian miner North Ltd said on Friday it had bought a majority stake in Canada's biggest iron ore producer, boasting it was now a big-league supplier of the world's major steel-making commodity.
North said it had paid US$230 million for a 59.3 percent stake in the Iron Ore Co. of Canada (IOCC).
"This purchase...positions North as a major player in the world's iron ore industry," North managing director Campbell Anderson told a news conference.
North already reaps 14.7 million tonnes of iron ore each year from its majority-owned Robe River mine in northwest Australia. Its IOCC stake adds about nine million tonnes a year.
IOCC, with its higher quality iron ore and presence in U.S. and European markets, will expand North's global reach which has so far been confined to steel-hungry Asia, Anderson said.
"As an established producer, IOCC will have immediate positive impact on North's earnings...," he said.
North's announcement follows two recent acquisitions in copper and zinc and is part of a strategy to firm up sagging profits and become a global player in metal commodities.
Weak metals prices and a strong Australian dollar have sent earnings into a slide in recent years, intensifying North's search for new growth opportunities.
North posted on Friday a 55 percent rise on net profit for the six months to December 31, largely due to improved performances in its iron ore, copper and uranium operations.

It said the second half of 1996/97 (July/June) would be even stronger and the outlook for 1997/98 brighter still, with the start-up in August of the huge Alumbrera copper-gold mine in Argentina. North owns 25 percent of the project.
But some stock analysts sounded a warning about North's latest foray, citing IOCC's high production costs and the uncertain outlook for iron ore.
"There's a risk of the iron ore price coming down in real terms in the next two to three years," one analyst told Reuters.
North conceded IOCC's production costs per tonne were relatively high, but said it was confident it could slash costs and foreshadowed major staff cuts.
"Changes in the workforce are subject to discussions with the unions, but we do see a considerable reduction," Anderson said, adding he did not anticipate union unrest.
But Bell Securities analyst Rob Craigie said he remained to be convinced that the costs could be pared back sufficently.
"Clearly they have ideas on how to reduce costs but (they are) certainly not convincing. They may be able to, but it's early days," Craigie said.
The stock market barely reacted to news of the acquisition and the interim profit announcement, both of which were widely anticipated.
North shares inched two cents higher from Thursday's close to end the week at A$3.94 (US$$3)
